Here in Britain, we almost never say a simple no. It feels far too rude. Instead, we have a whole collection of softer phrases. The most useful three words in the language are I'm afraid. I'm afraid I can't make it. I'm afraid I'm busy that evening. They don't mean we're scared, of course. They just tell the other person that bad news is coming, gently. Then there's I'd rather not, which is polite but very clear. And my best piece of advice: after you say no, offer something else. I can't do Friday, but I'd love to see you next week. That way, nobody feels let down.

For years I said yes to everything. Can you help with this report? Yes. Can you join this meeting? Sure. The result? I was swamped. I worked every weekend, and honestly, I did everything a little worse. Now, when someone asks for a favor at short notice, I have two answers. The first is: I'd prefer to help you next week, when I can do it properly. The second is: I can do it, but then this other project will have to wait. Which would you rather have? People respect that. My boss told me once that he'd rather have three things done well than ten things done badly. That changed everything for me.

I used to be the guy who said yes to everything. Drinks on Friday? Sure. Help you move house on Saturday? No worries. Then one night I'd said yes to three different plans, and I ended up bailing on my best mate's birthday. I sent him a message at nine o'clock. Big mistake. He was really let down, and he didn't answer me for a week. So I went to his place with all the ingredients and cooked him dinner, to make up for it. And I promised him something. Next time, I'd rather say no on Monday than bail on Saturday night. He said no hard feelings, and we're fine now. But I learned my lesson.
